chunks: Abu Ali Al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, from Safwan, from Abdillah ibn Muskhan, from Abu Baseer, who said:

I asked him (peace be upon him) about the one in Ihram who intends to perform a deed, so his companion says to him, 'By Allah, do not do it.' So he says, 'By Allah, I will do it.' So he opposes him a few times. Does it necessitate upon him what necessitates upon the one who quarrels? He (peace be upon him) said: 'No. Rather, what is meant by this is honoring his brother. Rather, that (penalty) is what was for the sake of Allah wherein is a disobedience.'

key_terms.إِكْرَامَ أَخِيهِ: Honoring his brother (a social gesture, not a legal vow)
key_terms.الْمُحْرِمِ: The one in the state of Ihram (ritual consecration for Hajj or Umrah)
key_terms.صَاحِبُ الْجِدَالِ: The one who quarrels/argues (implying a penalty for serious dispute)
key_terms.لِلَّهِ فِيهِ مَعْصِيَةٌ: For the sake of Allah wherein is a disobedience (distinguishing between social vows and religious obligations)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a person in Ihram who says 'By Allah I will do it' in response to a companion's urging?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Kafi clarifies that mutual swearing ('By Allah') between companions in Ihram regarding permissible acts is a social gesture of respect rather than a binding vow (kaffarah), provided the act itself is not sinful. Shia scholars emphasize the distinction between 'idhafah' (swearing for emphasis) and 'nadr' (vowing), noting that the penalty only applies if the core action constitutes disobedience to Allah, reflecting the juristic principle of leniency in Ihram rituals.
